slides.title: Chapter 11: The Blockchain
slides.sub: What a block holds, how blocks are named and linked, how a merkle tree vouches for them, and the test chains. Bitcoin Core 31.1 results are Recorded.
slides.notes: This deck explains the blockchain: the block and its 80-byte header, how a block is named and numbered, how blocks hold one another, how a merkle tree vouches for the transactions, and the test chains that practise all of it. Every example runs under Python 3.14.6 on the chapter's own library, and Bitcoin Core 31.1 was run on a test network, so its answers are Recorded and only read back here. The research package for chapter 11 holds the sources and the claims.

slides.title: The block and the chain
slides.sub: What a block holds, how it is named and numbered, and how blocks hold one another.

items.label: Block and header
The genesis block
Name, height, links
Forks

slides.notes: This part opens a block and looks at every field of its header. It then asks how a block is named, how it is numbered, and what links it to its parent, and it ends with the case of two children of one parent. The first block, with its newspaper headline, is the story of the part.

slides.title: A block is a header and its transactions
slides.sub: Like a parcel: a label on top, a count of the items, then the items themselves

rows: g, s = L.chainparams_genesis('main'), {n: R['b4_blocks'][str(n)]['size'] for n in (1, 2, 3, 4)}
items.label: Recorded: Core 31.1 regtest; the genesis constants are saved from chainparams.cpp

items: Row 2: the first block is 80 + 1 + 204 = 285 bytes; blocks 1 to 4 then hold 250, 472, 694 and 915 bytes
Rows 3 and 4: the book's size field is a prefix Bitcoin Core writes in its block file, which it scrambles with a key
Row 5: the counter takes 1, 3 or 5 bytes; at 60 bytes at least per transaction a block holds 16,666 at most

slides.notes: A block is an 80-byte header, a count of transactions, and the transactions. The first block of the test chain measured 285 bytes: 80 for the header, 1 for the count and 204 for its one transaction. The size field shown in the book's table is not part of the block but a prefix that Bitcoin Core writes in front of each block in its block files, which since release 28.0 are scrambled with a random key.
slides.take: A block is a header, a count and transactions; the size field is file storage

slides.title: The 80-byte header and its six fields
slides.sub: Fields are stored little-endian, and the version is now a set of flags

items: 80 bytes
50,000 headers in a block
version = flags

rows: L.header(L.raw('mempool_header_0.txt'))['version'], h['version'], seen('bip-0009.mediawiki', 'The top 3 bits of such blocks must be 001')
items.label: Recorded: Core 31.1 regtest; blocks 277,315 and 840,000 are saved from mempool.space

items: Rows 2 and 3: block 277,315 has an 80-byte header; its version 2 is stored as 02000000 and its previous hash reversed
Row 4: block 840,000 has version 0x2a5fe000: the top three bits are 001 (BIP 9), the other bits are flags
Row 5: the first block had version 1 and this one 2, so the book's name version number no longer fits

slides.notes: The header holds six fields in 80 bytes: version, previous block hash, merkle root, time, bits and nonce, with numbers stored least significant byte first and hashes shown reversed. A block may be 4,000,000 bytes, so it can be 50,000 times its header. The version is no longer a counter: BIP 9 sets the top three bits to 001 for blocks that signal, and the remaining bits are flags.
slides.take: Six fields fill 80 bytes, and the version is now a set of flags

slides.title: Time, target and nonce
slides.sub: Like asking eleven clocks and trusting the middle one

items.label: Recorded: Core 31.1 regtest; block 277,315 is saved from mempool.space

items: Row 2: time counts seconds from 1970 and runs out in 2106; a block may be at most 7,200 seconds ahead of the clock
Row 3: the median of the last 11 times, 1792052132 by our code and the node, is the floor; block 277,315 is 1,651 s above
Rows 4 and 5: bits 1d00ffff is difficulty 1; block 277,315 needed 1,180,941,215 full nonce ranges, hence the extra nonce

slides.notes: The timestamp of a block must be greater than the median of the previous 11 block times and at most two hours ahead of the node's clock. The target is stored compactly in bits: 1d00ffff means a target of 0xffff followed by zeros, which is difficulty 1. Block 277,315 had a difficulty of 1,180,923,195, so its proof of work needed far more than the 4,294,967,296 values of the 32-bit nonce, which is why miners also change an extra nonce.
slides.take: The median of 11 times is the floor; the nonce alone is too small

slides.title: A block's name is the hash of its header
slides.sub: Like a fingerprint: taken from the block, never printed inside it

rows: g['hash'] in g['block_hex'], L.rev(g['hash']) in g['block_hex'], len(g['block_hex']) // 2
items.label: Recorded: Core 31.1 regtest; the header of block 0 is saved from mempool.space

items: Row 2: SHA-256 run twice over the 80 header bytes gives 000000000019d668...; run once it gives 6dd6c571...
Rows 3 and 4: the 285 bytes of the first block hold its hash neither way round; the next header holds it
Row 6: blocks 0, 277,315 and 840,000 have 10, 15 and 19 leading zeros in hex: the proof of work

slides.notes: The identifier of a block is the double SHA-256 of its 80-byte header, shown byte-reversed. The hash is not stored in the block itself: the 285 bytes of the first block contain it neither way round, and it is the next block's header that carries it. The leading zeros grow with the difficulty, from 10 hex digits in block 0 to 19 in block 840,000.
slides.take: The name is computed from the header and carried by the next block

slides.title: Back-links make the history hard to change
slides.sub: Like layers in a glacier: disturb an old layer and every later one is disturbed

rows: hs = R['b3_headers_480_489']; p = [L.header(h) for h in hs]; w = R['b3_chainwork']
[p[i]['prev'] == p[i - 1]['hash'] for i in range(1, 10)].count(True), len(p), p[0]['prev'][:8], p[9]['hash'][:8]
[int(w[str(i)], 16) for i in range(4)], L.work('207fffff'), int(R['b2_info']['chainwork'], 16), 2 * 501
items.label: Recorded: Core 31.1 regtest

items: Row 2: in ten consecutive blocks, 9 of 9 previous-hash fields point to the hash of the block before
Row 3: changing block 3 changes its own hash, breaks the link in block 4, and 7 blocks would have to be re-mined
Row 4: on regtest each block adds work 2, so 501 blocks hold 1002; on the main chain it is far larger

slides.notes: Each header carries the hash of its parent, so the chain is a list in which every link depends on everything before it. On the test chain, ten consecutive headers linked correctly, and changing the fourth changed its hash, broke the link in the fifth, and meant that seven blocks would have to be mined again. The work of the chain is the sum of the work of its blocks, so the chain with the most work wins.
slides.take: Changing one old block means mining it and all later blocks again

slides.title: Forks: two children, one parent
slides.sub: Like two branches on one trunk: the tree grows on along the stronger one

items: Row 2: two blocks were mined at height 511 on one parent: the same height, different children
Row 3: a block built on one child makes it the active chain at 512; the other stays a valid fork
Row 4: from 6 blocks behind, an attacker with 10 percent catches up with chance 0.0002428, one with 30 percent 0.1321

items.title: Chance to catch up from 6 blocks behind

rows: f['height1'], f['height2'], f['child1'] != f['child2'], f['prev1'] == f['prev2'] == f['parent']
[(t['height'], t['branchlen'], t['status']) for t in f['tips_after']], f['active_is'] == f['extension']
items.label: Recorded: Core 31.1 regtest, and the formula of the paper

slides.notes: Two miners can find a block at about the same time, and then one parent has two children at the same height. The test node held both and called the one with more work active and the other a valid fork, and a block on top of one child settled it. The chance that an attacker catches up falls quickly with the number of blocks: with 10 percent of the power it is 0.2045873 from one block behind and 0.0002428 from six.
slides.take: A fork is settled by more work, and an old block is soon safe

slides.title: Merkle trees
slides.sub: How one 32-byte root vouches for every transaction in a block, and where the tree is weak.

items.label: Building the tree
Proof by a short path
Two weaknesses
Ralph Merkle

slides.notes: This part is about the hash tree that sits between a block's transactions and its header. It shows how the root is built, how a short path proves that one transaction belongs, and where the tree is weak: a duplicated hash and a 64-byte transaction. The story is that of its inventor, Ralph Merkle.

slides.title: The merkle tree: many transactions, one root
slides.sub: Like a knockout draw: pairs are matched until one name is left at the top

rows: b = R['b4_blocks']['4']; i = [bytes.fromhex(t)[::-1] for t in b['txids']]; h = L.sha256d
[len(l) for l in L.merkle_levels(b['txids'])], h(h(i[0] + i[1]) + h(i[2] + i[3]))[::-1].hex() == b['merkleroot']
[len(l) for l in L.merkle_levels(o['txids'])], L.merkle_root(o['txids']) == o['merkleroot']
items.label: Recorded: Core 31.1 regtest

items: Row 2: four transactions give levels of 4, 2 and 1 hashes, and hashing the two pairs gives the header's root
Rows 3 and 4: three transactions give levels 3, 2 and 1: the last hash is paired with itself; the root is the header's
Row 5: adding a copy of the last transaction gives the same root, so the odd one is simply duplicated

slides.notes: The transaction ids of a block are hashed in pairs, level by level, until one hash is left, and that merkle root goes into the header. For four transactions the levels have 4, 2 and 1 hashes, and the test node's root matched our own. When a level has an odd count, its last hash is paired with itself, which is why a copy of the last transaction gives the same root.
slides.take: Pairs are hashed upward; an odd hash is paired with itself

slides.title: A merkle proof is a short path of hashes
slides.sub: Like checking a ledger page against a signed total using only the subtotals beside it

items: Row 2: to prove transaction 10 of 16 only 4 hashes are needed, 128 bytes, and they lead back to the root
Row 3: a path grows with the logarithm: 320, 384 and 448 bytes for 1,024, 4,096 and 16,000 transactions
Row 4: with the 80-byte header a proof is 528 bytes, so a full block is 7,576 times larger, not 10,000

items.title: Bytes of proof path by transactions in a block

rows: b = R['b4_blocks']['16']; ids = b['txids']; p = L.merkle_path(ids, 10)
len(p), 32 * len(p), [r for s, r in p], L.follow_path(ids[10], p) == b['merkleroot']
items.label: Recorded: Core 31.1 regtest; the sizes follow from the depth

slides.notes: A light client can check that a transaction is in a block with only the hashes along its path to the root, one for each level. For transaction 10 of 16 that is 4 hashes, 128 bytes, and following them reproduced the root of the header. The path grows with the logarithm of the block, 448 bytes for 16,000 transactions, so with the header a proof is 528 bytes; the book's claim of almost 10,000 times smaller is really 7,576 times.
slides.take: A proof is a few hashes, and the book's ratio of 10,000 is 7,576

slides.title: Two weaknesses of the merkle tree
slides.sub: Like two different shopping lists that give the same receipt total

items: the last hash is repeated
64-byte transactions

rows: ids = [L.sha256d(bytes([i])).hex() for i in range(1, 7)]; b = ids + [ids[4], ids[5]]
m['n_original'], m['n_mutated'], m['same_header'], m['submit_mutated'], m['submit_original'], m['tip_is_original']
len(bytes.fromhex(k[0]) + bytes.fromhex(k[1])), 240 // 4, seen('bip-0054.md', 'exactly 64 bytes are invalid')
items.label: Recorded: Core 31.1 regtest; the BIP 54 passage is saved

items: Row 2: six transactions and the same six with the last two repeated give one root: two blocks, one header
Row 4: given the 4-transaction version of a 3-transaction block, the node refused it and kept the original
Row 5: an inner node is the hash of 64 bytes; BIP 54 makes a 64-byte transaction invalid so none can pose as one

slides.notes: Because an odd hash is paired with itself, a list with the last transactions repeated has the same root as the original, so two different blocks can share one header. Bitcoin Core refuses the mutated block with bad-txns-duplicate, and on the test chain it kept the original. The second weakness is that an inner node is the hash of 64 bytes, so a transaction of exactly 64 bytes could be mistaken for one, which BIP 54 forbids.
slides.take: The tree has two known weaknesses, and the node defends against both

slides.title: One small hash that vouches for a list
slides.sub: The story of 5 January 1982: who, where, when and what to read next

items.cap: Ralph Merkle - david.orban (Flickr), CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: On 5 January 1982 United States patent 4309569 is published: Ralph Merkle's hash tree, assigned to Stanford University (row 1)
He had described tree authentication in 1980; Nakamoto's paper keeps only the root of such a tree in each header
The 40 transactions of block 277,315 hash up to the root in its header (row 3)

items.label: executed on saved sources and a real block saved from mempool.space

items.who: Ralph Merkle, the cryptographer who patented the hash tree, and Stanford University, the assignee of the patent
items.where: Stanford University in California; United States patent 4309569, published on 5 January 1982

slides.notes: Ralph Merkle patented the hash tree in 1979, and the United States patent 4309569 was published on 5 January 1982 with Stanford University as assignee. In 1980 he wrote about tree authentication, and Satoshi Nakamoto's paper hashes the transactions of a block in such a tree and keeps only the root in the header. The 40 transactions of block 277,315 hashed in pairs up six levels to the root in its header.

They run the same code as the main chain but with different rules, prefixes and ports, and each solved a problem of the one before it. slides.notes: The same program runs five chains, chosen by an option, each with its own data directory, port and address prefixes. The book's tip says that test addresses begin with m, n or tb1, but the test chains also use the prefix 2 for script addresses, and regtest uses bcrt1. Regtest halves its reward every 150 blocks, so 500 blocks earned 12,462.5 coins, as the book shows. No connection to a real network was made.
slides.take: One program runs five chains; the prefixes are more than the book lists

slides.sub: Testnet3 is far past one block in ten minutes, and testnet4 follows BIP 94

items.label: executed on the saved chain parameters and heights saved from mempool.space

slides.notes: Testnet coins are worth nothing, so nothing stops a miner from flooding the chain. Testnet3 lets a block use minimum difficulty after twenty idle minutes, and its height is 6.3 times what one block in ten minutes would give; the book's size of 30 GB is far out of date too. Testnet4, specified in BIP 94, has its own genesis block and rules against the flooding. The heights are public figures; no test network was synchronised here.
slides.take: Testnet3 was flooded; testnet4 has rules against it

slides.notes: On 4 May 2024 Jameson Lopp published how the minimum-difficulty rule of testnet3 lets miners create hundreds of blocks in a day. Testnet4 had its genesis block on 3 May 2024, and BIP 94, written by Fabian Jahr, bounds the time of the first block of a period; Bitcoin Core 28.0 added the network. BIP 94 notes that three years of blocks were mined on testnet3 in a few weeks, and testnet3 is now 33 times as long as testnet4.

slides.title: Signet: blocks need a signature
slides.sub: Like a club with a doorman: only someone he knows may open the door

items: challenge: 1 of 2 keys
magic 0a03cf40
challenge 51: anyone signs

items.label: Recorded: Core 31.1 regtest; the signet height is a public figure saved from mempool.space

items: Row 2: the default signet's challenge is 71 bytes, 1 of 2 keys must sign: either of the two operators can sign a block
Row 3: the four magic bytes are the start of the hash of the challenge: 0a03cf40; the challenge 51 gives 54d26fbd
Rows 4 and 5: both signets share one genesis; the default is at height 326,440, 2.27 times the book's 143,619

items.body: NOT EXECUTED: mining a block on the public signet.

slides.notes: On a signet a block is valid only if it carries a signature that satisfies a challenge script, so the operators decide who may make blocks and the chain stays calm. The default signet's challenge is a one-of-two multisig, which is why the book says two contributors run it; a signet with the challenge 51 can be signed by anyone and ran on the test node. The network magic is derived from the challenge, so every signet has its own.
slides.take: A signet block needs a signature, so the chain stays calm

slides.sub: The story of 20 March 2019: who, where, when and what to read next

items: On 20 March 2019 BIP 325 is assigned to Karl-Johan Alm and Anthony Towns: a block needs a signature on a challenge (row 1)
Bitcoin Core 0.21.0 adds signet; the magic is the hash of the challenge (row 2), so every custom signet has its own
The public signet is at 2.27 times the book's 143,619 blocks (row 3); NOT EXECUTED: mining on it

items.label: executed on saved sources and the Core 31.1 record (Recorded)

items.who: Karl-Johan Alm and Anthony Towns, the authors of BIP 325
items.where: the bitcoin/bips repository, and Bitcoin Core 0.21.0

items.body: Stand-in picture: a signet ring, not the BIP.

slides.notes: BIP 325, Signet, was assigned on 20 March 2019 to Karl-Johan Alm and Anthony Towns: a block is valid only if it carries a solution to a challenge script, so the creators of a signet decide who may make blocks. Bitcoin Core 0.21.0 added the support, and personal signets are possible with the option -signetchallenge. The network magic is the start of the hash of the challenge, so every signet has its own, and the public one is 2.27 times as long as the book's listing.
